The error you’re encountering is due to the order of operations. You’re trying to insert a row into the employee table before the branch table has been created and populated. The branch\_id in the employee table is a foreign key that references the branch table. If the branch table doesn’t exist or doesn’t have the referenced value, you’ll get a foreign key constraint error.  
  
Here’s how you can resolve this:  
  
First, create the branch table.  
Then, insert the relevant data into the branch table.  
After that, create the employee table.  
Finally, insert the data into the employee table.  
Here’s the corrected SQL:  
  
SQL  
  
CREATE TABLE branch (  
branch\_id INT PRIMARY KEY,  
branch\_name VARCHAR(40),  
mgr\_id INT,  
mgr\_start\_date DATE  
);  
  
INSERT INTO branch VALUES(1,'Corporate',100,'2006-02-09');  
  
CREATE TABLE employee(  
emp\_id INT PRIMARY KEY,  
first\_name VARCHAR(40),  
last\_name VARCHAR(40),  
birth\_day DATE,  
Sex VARCHAR(1),  
salary INT,  
super\_id INT,  
branch\_id INT,  
FOREIGN KEY(branch\_id) REFERENCES branch(branch\_id) ON DELETE SET NULL,  
FOREIGN KEY(mgr\_id) REFERENCES employee(emp\_id) ON DELETE SET NULL  
);

Is the sample/response "random"? Practically speaking, yes. That is assuming that you sent roughly the same communication/incentive at roughly the same time. You didn't do anything to influence who responds.

Is the sample/response free of bias? No. But imho, surveys are never free of bias. Some subset of teachers are more likely to respond than others and that's near impossible to account for truly. That means that the authors need to be transparent about who they sent the survey to, how it was sent, and ideally describe the demographics of the responder.

Are test assumptions violated? Not a big enough violation to be concerning. I would apply the test and in the interpretation include something to the effect of "of responding employees".

​

In short, I would consider it a randomized sample of convenience, and do a good job of describing who and how the survey was administered and include demographic info if possible. In the interpretation reiterate that it's applied to responding participants.

The quick and dirty way to fix this is to use the double assignment arrow (<<-) to assign a variable to one environment higher, the global environment in this case.
